item.title: New NASA Artemis payloads to study moon's terrain, radiation, history
item.description: NASA announced Tuesday the selection of three new science investigations that will strengthen humanity's understanding and exploration of the moon. As part of the agency's CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative and Artemis campaign, American companies will deliver these research payloads to the lunar surface no earlier than 2028.

item.title: Not to be outdone by OpenAI, Apple is reportedly developing an AI wearable
item.description: Should this wearable materialize, it could be released as early as 2027, according to a report on the device.

item.title: Piercing crocodile close-up wins ecology photo competition
item.description: A striking shot of biting flies on the head of a crocodile is among the winning entries in the British Ecological Society’s annual Capturing Ecology photography competition

item.title: Judge orders stop to FBI search of devices seized from Washington Post reporter
item.description: Order says gov't must stop search while court reviews Washington Post motions.

item.title: Natural ovulation the best option before an IVF frozen embryo transfer
item.description: Women using frozen embryos as part of their IVF treatment can either choose to use a medicated cycle or their natural one to prepare their uterus for a pregnancy. Now, scientists have found that the latter option seems to carry fewer risks

item.title: Sources: Project SGLang spins out as RadixArk with $400M valuation as inference market explodes
item.description: SGLang, which originated as an open source research project at Ion Stoica’s UC Berkeley lab, has raised capital from Accel.

item.title: Millions of people imperiled through sign-in links sent by SMS
item.description: Even well-known services with millions of users are exposing sensitive data.

item.title: Artificial intelligence in manufacturing rocket parts
item.description: Artificial Intelligence, or AI, promises many benefits in all domains, and rocketry is no different. The European Space Agency's Future Launchers Preparatory Program (FLPP) is investigating the use of AI to develop better processes and even whole new shapes in materials that could be used on rockets or spacecraft of the future.

item.title: Snow is vital for the Pyrenees, and it's disappearing fast
item.description: Snow is a defining feature of mountain ranges, and of winter itself for much of the world. But beyond its scenic value, snow plays a vital role in mountain ecosystems, as well as a range of human socioeconomic activity, and it is one of the climatic elements most sensitive to global warming. In recent decades, its quantity, duration and behavior have all changed significantly.

item.title: mRNA cancer vaccine shows protection at 5-year follow-up, Moderna and Merck say
item.description: The vaccines are tailor-made to target each patient's unique cancer.

item.title: New analysis suggests carbon markets must account for storage duration in pricing removals
item.description: Carbon dioxide removal technologies are becoming increasingly important for climate action, but their differing storage times matter for policy design. A new study published in Environmental and Resource Economics by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) provides guidance based on economic principles. While non-permanent carbon storage plays a valuable role as economies transition away from fossil fuels, its contribution is less valuable than permanent storage; this should be reflected in carbon pricing schemes that aim to incentivize the ramping-up of removals.

item.title: A timeline of the US semiconductor market in 2025
item.description: From leadership changes at legacy semiconductor companies to wishy washy policy around chip exports, a lot happened last year.

item.title: Todoist’s app now lets you add tasks to your to-do list by speaking to its AI
item.description: The feature, now public, lets you create to-do's and action items by speaking naturally to the app's AI.

item.title: Massive cloud with metallic winds discovered orbiting mystery object
item.description: Sweeping winds of vaporized metals have been found in a massive cloud that dimmed the light of a star for nearly nine months. This discovery, made with the Gemini South telescope in Chile, one half of the International Gemini Observatory, offers a rare glimpse into the chaotic and dynamic processes still shaping planetary systems long after their formation.

item.title: Beneath Antarctica’s largest ice shelf, a hidden ocean is revealing its secrets
item.description: A four-year record from the heart of the Ross Ice Shelf shows how subtle changes could shape future sea level rise, ocean ecosystems – and even our weather.

item.title: Apple plans to make Siri an AI chatbot, report says
item.description: Siri could look more like ChatGPT than its current state as an integrated feature across Apple products.

item.title: Anthropic revises Claude’s ‘Constitution,’ and hints at chatbot consciousness
item.description: The newly revised document offers a roadmap for what Anthropic says is a safer and more helpful chatbot experience.

item.title: Trump FCC threatens to enforce equal-time rule on late-night talk shows
item.description: FCC disputes long-standing view that the shows are exempt from equal-time rule.

item.title: Pine bark removes pharmaceutical residues from wastewater—an affordable way to keep antibiotics out of nature
item.description: Researchers at the University of Oulu, Finland, have developed a pine-bark–based water-treatment medium that efficiently removes antibiotics as well as residues of blood-pressure and antidepressant medicines from wastewater treatment plant effluent. A new doctoral thesis reports promising results with a simple and low-cost method in which pine bark was modified with iron.

item.title: The problem with revisiting Tomb Raider: Reacclimating to tank controls
item.description: For our C:\ArsGames series, we look at the controls conundrum of early 3D.

item.title: 'Extreme cold': Winter storm forecast to slam huge expanse of US
item.description: A winter storm bringing very cold temperatures is expected to slam a massive stretch of the United States this week with more than 175 million people facing the prospect of power outages and travel disruptions.

item.title: Kioxia's memory is "sold out" for 2026, prolonging a "high-end and expensive phase"
item.description: Kioxia is spinning up more manufacturing capacity, but relief will come slowly.

item.title: Irony alert: Hallucinated citations found in papers from NeurIPS, the prestigious AI conference
item.description: Research from startup GPTZero points to the impossible problem prestigious conferences face in the age of AI slop.

item.title: Q&A: How AI changes NASA's search for life in outer space
item.description: Alicja Ostrowska's doctoral thesis "Life and AI at NASA" examines how artificial intelligence is transforming the way science is conducted within some of the world's most ambitious space projects. The study investigates how AI is used in NASA's missions exploring the conditions for present or past life on other planets and moons and what this means for how knowledge is produced. The research is based on fieldwork with scientists and engineers at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center.

item.title: Webb finds young sun-like star forging common crystals and flinging them into its outer disk
item.description: Astronomers have long sought evidence to explain why comets at the outskirts of our own solar system contain crystalline silicates, since crystals require intense heat to form and these "dirty snowballs" spend most of their time in the ultracold Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud. Now, looking outside our solar system, NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has returned the first conclusive evidence that links how those conditions are possible.

item.title: Watch a robot swarm "bloom" like a garden
item.description: The Swarm Garden: An array of modular robot agents that adapt to changing conditions for living architecture.

item.title: Compact electron accelerator offers new approach for treating PFAS-contaminated water
item.description: So-called forever chemicals or PFAS compounds are a growing environmental problem. An innovative approach to treating PFAS‐contaminated water and soil now comes from accelerator physics: high‐energy electrons can break down PFAS molecules into harmless components through a process called radiolysis.

item.title: Spotify won court order against Anna’s Archive, taking down .org domain
item.description: Lawsuit was filed under seal; Anna's Archive wasn't notified until after takedown.

item.title: Another Jeff Bezos company has announced plans to develop a megaconstellation
item.description: With data speeds of up to 6Tbps, one could stream a lot of HD movies.

item.title: Balkan wild rivers in steady decline: Study
item.description: Thousands of kilometers of Balkan rivers have been damaged in recent years, a study published Wednesday found, as hydropower development, dams and sediment extraction drive a "steady erosion" of some of Europe's last pristine waterways.

item.title: Meteorologists blame a stretched polar vortex, moisture, lack of sea ice for dangerous winter blast
item.description: Warm Arctic waters and cold continental land are combining to stretch the dreaded polar vortex in a way that will send much of the United States a devastating dose of winter weather later this week with swaths of painful subzero temperatures, heavy snow and powerline-toppling ice.

item.title: Radio telescopes on the moon could let us observe dozens of black hole shadows
item.description: We now have direct images of two supermassive black holes: M87* and Sag A*. The fact that we can capture such images is remarkable, but they might be the only black holes we can observe. That is, unless we take radio astronomy to a whole new level.

item.title: NZ is again being soaked this summer – record ocean heat helps explain it
item.description: Understanding what is happening deep beneath the ocean surface is key to understanding the weather patterns we are experiencing on land.

item.title: Massive black hole mystery unlocked by researchers
item.description: It's one of astronomy's great mysteries: how did black holes get so big, so massive, so quickly. An answer to this cosmic conundrum has now been provided by researchers at Ireland's Maynooth University (MU) and reported today in Nature Astronomy.

item.title: Studying massive and mysterious young protostars with Hubble
item.description: Baby pictures are some of a family's most cherished artifacts. The same thing can be said of the Hubble Space Telescope and the infant stars it immortalizes in its scientific portraits. But while we know how babies are conceived and how they form in great detail, the same can't be said for star formation.

item.title: Despite its steep environmental costs, AI might also help save the planet
item.description: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence has sharply increased electricity and water consumption, raising concerns about the technology's environmental footprint and carbon emissions. But the story is more complicated than that.

item.title: US forests store record carbon as natural and human factors combine
item.description: U.S. forests have stored more carbon in the past two decades than at any time in the last century, an increase attributable to a mix of natural factors and human activity, finds a new study.

item.title: Here's Volvo's new EX60 $60,000 electric midsize SUV
item.description: The EX60 goes into production in April 2026.

item.title: Q&A: Wildfire in protected Northwest forests highlights need for strategy updates
item.description: The Northwest Forest Plan, adopted in 1994, helped quell mounting tensions between timber companies and environmentalists. It protected large swaths of old-growth forest in Washington, Oregon and California to preserve habitat for endangered species, including the Northern spotted owl and marbled murrelet.

item.title: Grains of sand prove people—not glaciers—transported Stonehenge rocks
item.description: Ask people how Stonehenge was built and you'll hear stories of sledges, ropes, boats and sheer human determination to haul stones from across Britain to Salisbury Plain, in south-west England. Others might mention giants, wizards, or alien assistance to explain the transport of Stonehenge's stones, which come from as far as Wales and Scotland.

item.title: Safeguarding the Winter Olympics-Paralympics against climate change
item.description: New research into the impact of climate change on snow sports provides recommendations to increase the climate-resilience of the Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games.

item.title: World's first high-resolution global leaf chlorophyll map can closely track plant health
item.description: A research team led by Profs. Li Jing and Liu Qinhuo from the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) has developed the world's first global, high-resolution map of leaf chlorophyll content (LCC), providing a new method for closely tracking plant health and ecosystem productivity worldwide. The study was recently published in Scientific Data.

item.title: Our earliest vertebrate ancestors may have had four eyes
item.description: Extraordinary fossils of 518-million-year-old jawless fish, among the earliest known vertebrates, appear to show that these animals had two pairs of eyes

item.title: Oldest known rock art is a 68,000-year-old hand stencil with claws
item.description: Newly discovered rock art sites in Sulawesi, Indonesia, that date to nearly 68,000 years ago are thought to be the oldest rock art in the world, pre-dating Neanderthal hand stencils in Spain by 1100 years

item.title: Ape-like hominin Paranthropus was more adaptable than we thought
item.description: A fossil discovery in northern Ethiopia expands the known range of Paranthropus, a genus of strong-jawed hominins that lived around 2 million years ago, and suggests they lived in a range of habitats

item.title: Bird retinas work without oxygen, and now scientists know how
item.description: The light-sensitive tissue of birds’ eyes is not supplied with oxygen by blood vessels – instead, it powers itself with a flood of sugar, and this may have evolutionary benefits

item.title: Critical Atlantic Ocean currents kept going during last ice age, microfossils suggest
item.description: During the last ice age, the Atlantic Ocean's powerful current system remained active and continued to transport warm, salty water from the tropics to the North Atlantic despite extensive ice cover across much of the Northern Hemisphere, finds new research led by UCL scientists.

item.description: YouTube Shorts viewers might soon see AI versions of their favorite creators when scrolling through their feeds.

item.title: The world is in water bankruptcy, UN scientists report—here's what that means
item.description: The world is now using so much fresh water amid the consequences of climate change that it has entered an era of water bankruptcy, with many regions no longer able to bounce back from frequent water shortages.

item.title: Legs made for a Mars landing
item.description: To land on the right foot on the Red Planet, European engineers have been dropping a skeleton of the four-legged ExoMars descent module at various speeds and heights on simulated Martian surfaces.

item.description: The AI startup is on track to announce its first hardware device in the second half of this year, OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane said during an interview Davos.

item.title: Astronomers discover a companion cluster to Czernik 38
item.description: Astronomers from the National Research Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics (NRIAG) in Cairo, Egypt, have investigated a young open cluster known as Czernik 38. As a result, they found a new open cluster, which turns out to be a companion to Czernik 38. The discovery was detailed in a paper published Jan. 14 on the arXiv pre-print server.

item.title: Dredging sand and silt has consequences for the North Sea
item.description: Through sand extraction and the disposal of dredged harbor silt, about 200 million tons of sediment are relocated every year in the coastal waters of the North Sea. The Wadden Sea is particularly strongly affected. This is the result of a new study by the Helmholtz Center Hereon, which for the first time evaluated comprehensive data on dredging activities along the North Sea coasts.

item.title: Enceladus plumes may hold a clear clue to ocean habitability
item.description: How can scientists estimate the pH level of Enceladus' subsurface ocean without landing on its surface? This is what a study recently posted to the arXiv preprint server hopes to address as a team of scientists from Japan investigated new methods for sampling the plumes of Enceladus and have provided more accurate measurements of its pH levels. This study has the potential to help scientists better understand the subsurface ocean conditions on Enceladus and whether it's suitable for life as we know it.

item.description: Buzz Aldrin, the second man and only one of 12 to ever walk on the moon, turns 96 today. He's just one of four living moonwalkers and the oldest remaining astronaut still making trips around the sun.

item.description: The world is entering an era of "global water bankruptcy" with rivers, lakes and aquifers depleting faster than nature can replenish them, a United Nations research institute said on Tuesday.

item.description: NASA's Suni Williams—one of two astronauts stuck for months at the International Space Station—has retired.

item.title: Solar flares triggered by cascading magnetic avalanches, new observations reveal
item.description: Just as avalanches on snowy mountains start with the movement of a small quantity of snow, the ESA-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has discovered that a solar flare is triggered by initially weak disturbances that quickly become more violent. This rapidly evolving process creates a 'sky' of raining plasma blobs that continue to fall even after the flare subsides.
